Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Worker
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Vignette:
Marcus Vance had been thirty-eight when the assault occurred. He was reviewing paperwork for a caseload transfer in a small, windowless conference room off the main hall of a downtown community center when the heavy door clicked shut. The corridor’s ambient noise faded, and Marcus felt the space narrow around his shoulders. The assailant entered without warning, and he remembered the exact moment the air grew thick. Time stretched; the wall clock ticked slower than it should have, and every minute that passed without a knock felt like a silent threat building toward him. He had come to believe that when something took longer than expected, something bad was already underway. Afterward, he pushed the memories down, trying to force them out of his mind, but they kept surfacing during quiet moments. When he finally spoke of it, the terror rose in his chest just as it had then, raw and unfiltered, yet no matter how he tried to articulate it, the words caught in his throat. He knew what had happened, but he could not find the right way to say it. Over the following weeks and months, his habits formed quietly but firmly. He began checking behind him as he walked, his eyes darting over his shoulder to see if someone was following, a steady practice that sat alongside his daily commute. He avoided going to unfamiliar places, steering clear of new clinics, restaurants, or parking garages because he could not assess the danger in spaces he had not yet mapped. The conference room’s tight walls sat with his awareness of confinement; he started declining invitations to small meeting rooms and preferred open office doors at his own social work practice. His practice, nestled in a mid-rise building, became a landscape of familiar thresholds. He managed his caseload from a corner desk with a wide view, stepping out only when the route was known. At work, the delays in his schedule accumulated into a familiar weight. When a client arrived a few minutes late, or when referral paperwork piled up longer than expected, Marcus would sit rigid at his desk, certain that the postponement signaled an approaching problem. He ruminated often, replaying the assault not just as a memory, but as an unresolved debt, turning the question of how to get even with his assailant into a quiet, persistent calculus. His wife, Elena, watched these patterns settle into their routine. They stopped accepting last-minute plans, opting instead for the familiar routes and known faces. At home, he would sit in the large living room rather than the cozy study, keeping the hallway behind him visible. His avoidance and his heightened awareness occupied the same days without crowding each other out. Now at fifty-three, Marcus sits in a therapist’s office, the chairs arranged to keep the door open and the space unconfined. He had finally come in after a client meeting in a glass-walled conference room triggered a wave of dread that left him unable to speak for the rest of the afternoon. The shame washed over him again, sharp and sudden, as he tried to explain the incident to the receptionist, only to find his voice failing him entirely. He does not seek to erase the past, but to quiet the constant scanning and the heavy certainty that time, like the conference room door, can close without warning. He hopes to reclaim the ability to move through unfamiliar places without bracing for threat, and to stop the slow, daily accumulation of delays from feeling like warnings. Most of all, he wants the terror and the shame to stop rising together, leaving him enough room to breathe, enough words to say what happened, and enough peace to let the question of justice rest.
